name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Yusuf and I farm 60 hectares of our own in the hills above Kelby, plus grazing rights on the common hill. We run 650 ewes and 40 suckler cows, and we grow oats and turnips on the low fields for winter feed. In spring it's lambing day and night; the rest of the year it's gathering sheep off the hill with the dogs, fencing, and getting the oats in when the weather allows. Yusuf also drives part-time for the auction mart, moving stock for other farmers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you manage the business side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the books and the forms, mostly at night. I use an AI app now and then to check the forecast and the lamb prices at the mart, and once to help me write a grant application, though I checked every word. The hard part is the hill payments, the environmental money we get for looking after the land. They've been cut twice in four years, and without them a hill farm like ours doesn't pay. We have two children, Hana and Adam, and a mortgage on the house and the low fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say most of it was talk, which is what I expected. The forecast app is useful, and that's about it for a hill farm. At the mart I'd say the hill payments matter far more to us than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries stay exactly where they are. If the hill payments are cut again, we lose about a fifth of our income, and that's the difference between paying the mortgage and not. Lamb prices have been fair this year, but you can't build a family's life on one fair year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming the hill as we do, with the same flock. I'd cut back at home now, no new car and a cheaper holiday with Yusuf's brother's family instead of a trip. And I'd turn the old stone barn into a small holiday let over the next two years, so we have money that doesn't depend on payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's a worry I carry every day, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the holiday let cost, and where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 25,000 for a simple conversion, which we don't have. We'd do most of the work ourselves with Yusuf's brothers, who are builders, and borrow the rest from the family rather than the bank. My father would say that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not depend on payments. How do you feel about getting them at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, if I'm honest. I don't like being paid by the government, I'd rather sell what I grow. But hill farms look after the land everyone walks on, and that's work too.

say: Most of the AI talk was **just talk**, as I expected.
The **hill payments** matter far more to us than any computer.
think: Another **payment cut** would take about a fifth of our income.
One **fair year** for lamb prices can't carry a family's life.
do: Keep farming the hill with **the same flock** of 650 ewes.
Cut back at home with **no new car** and a cheaper holiday.
Convert the **old stone barn** into a holiday let over two years.
feel: **Anxious**, carrying the same worry every day.
S0.quote: If the hill payments are cut again, we lose about a fifth of our income, and that's the difference between paying the mortgage and not.
fieldNote: Sara's anxiety comes from **payment cuts**, which already happened twice.
She is **uncomfortable** depending on government money, but defends it.
Her plan uses **family labour and loans**, not the bank.
She's practical and **unexcited** about AI, using it only when useful.

steps.text: Keep running 650 ewes and 40 suckler cows on the hill
Skip the new car and holiday with Yusuf's brother's family
Convert the old stone barn into a holiday let with family help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be useful once people have shown it works. If AI can fill in the hill payment forms without mistakes, I'd use it. But I'd tell younger farmers not to trust a machine with the land until they've seen it a few seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the change I'd fear isn't on my farm, it's in the government office. If they use AI to check every claim, they'll find every small mistake and cut payments for it. And the people who used to help farmers with forms, like Mr Rees at the advisory office, would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use the AI properly for the payment forms and records, maybe through the course the farmers' union runs in winter. I'd keep the flock and the cattle the same, since robots on the hill are a long way off. And I'd carry on with the holiday let, because that money doesn't depend on any office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. The farm isn't threatened, but the payments always are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Rees at the advisory office. What would losing him mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Rees has helped half the valley through payment forms for twenty years. He knows which fields flood and which hedges count. A farm in the hills never fits the rules exactly, and a computer would follow the rules exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your own week is that thinking work, the forms and records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a day a week in winter, less in summer. If AI took most of that, I'd get evenings with Hana and Adam back. So it isn't all bad, I'll give it that.

say: AI will be useful **once it's proven**, for example on payment forms.
Young farmers shouldn't trust a machine with the land until **a few seasons** pass.
think: The danger is a **government office** using AI to cut payments for small mistakes.
Helpers like **Mr Rees** at the advisory office would be gone.
do: Learn AI for **payment forms** on the farmers' union winter course.
Keep the **flock and cattle** the same, since hill robots are far off.
Carry on building the **holiday let** for income outside payments.
feel: **Anxious**, because the payments are always under threat.
A little **relieved** at getting evenings back from forms.
S1.quote: A farm in the hills never fits the rules exactly, and a computer would follow the rules exactly.
fieldNote: Sara fears **AI** in the **payment office** more than AI on her farm.
She values **human advisers** like Mr Rees who know the land.
She'd **learn the tools** once proven, true to her steady approach.
Her **holiday let** plan is her hedge against payment risk.

steps.text: Take the farmers' union winter course on AI for payment forms
Keep 650 ewes and 40 suckler cows on the same system
Finish the barn holiday let for income outside payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should slow down and think about families before companies. At the mosque and at the mart I'd tell people to look after each other, because no government will move fast enough. I wouldn't be shouting, but I'd be saying it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the hill payments would be one of the first things changed, maybe cut, once AI runs the government's thinking work in 2028. Then by 2031 the robots arrive, and big lowland farms with robots would produce lamb cheaper than we ever could. I think we'd lose most of our farm income within five years, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage as hard as we can, maybe 300 extra a month, while lamb prices last. I'd talk to Yusuf's brothers about all of us working together, sharing machines and maybe the land. And I'd push the holiday let to open within a year, even half-finished, because tourists will still want hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And angry that it's happening to children like mine who've done nothing wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots three years later. What happens to your farm in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the forms and the payment checks change overnight, and I don't know if that helps or hurts. The hands-on work, gathering sheep off a steep hill in fog, carries on for those three years. I'd use those years to get the holiday let paying and to get the family organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana and Adam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family and we'll be fine together, which is true if we stick together. I'd tell Hana to keep studying hard, because she wants to be a vet, and animals will still need vets. Adam is only nine, so I'd just keep him out of the worry.

say: We should think about **families before companies**.
People must **look after each other**, because no government moves fast enough.
think: **Hill payments** would be changed or cut once AI runs government thinking work.
I think we'd lose most of our **farm income** within five years.
do: Pay an **extra 300 a month** off the mortgage while lamb prices last.
Plan with **Yusuf's brothers** to share machines and maybe land.
Open the **holiday let** within a year, even half-finished.
feel: **Frightened**, and angry for children who've done nothing wrong.
S2.quote: I think we'd lose most of our farm income within five years, and that frightens me.
fieldNote: Sara expects to **lose most farm income** and says so plainly.
She looks to the **extended family** before any government help.
She sees the robot gap as **time to organise** the family and the let.
Her children's **future** shapes what she'd say and do.

steps.text: Pay an extra 300 a month off the mortgage
Plan with Yusuf's brothers to share machines and land
Open the barn holiday let within a year, even half-finished

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given some warning, so let's be sensible with it. I'd tell other hill farmers to make sure their land is paid for and their children have skills. I'd not join any protests, but I'd talk to anyone at the mart who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's still hard for us, but we'd have time to change what the farm earns from. AI in 2031 would change the payments, and robots in 2034 would push lamb prices down. By then I'd want the farm to be half holiday lets and half sheep, not all sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the barn holiday let properly by 2028 and maybe add a second one in the old cart shed by 2030. I'd use AI tools for the bookings and the forms once I've seen a neighbour use them well. And I'd sit down with Hana about vet school, making sure we save something every month toward it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frightened. I can see a path through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a farmer first. How would it feel to be half a holiday business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, I won't pretend otherwise. My father would say I'd become a hotel, but the sheep would still be on the hill. The farm would still be ours, which matters more than what we call it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the valley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Morgans, two farms up, who are in their sixties with no children coming home. They'd struggle to change anything in five years. I'd want Yusuf and the boys to help them gather the sheep while they work out what to do.

say: We've been given **some warning**, so be sensible with it.
Hill farmers should make sure their **land is paid for** and children have skills.
think: It's still hard, but we'd have **time to change** what the farm earns from.
By 2034 I'd want the farm **half holiday lets** and half sheep.
do: Finish the barn let by **2028** and add a second in the cart shed.
Use AI tools for **bookings and forms** once a neighbour proves them.
feel: **Worried** but less frightened, seeing a path through.
S3.quote: My father would say I'd become a hotel, but the sheep would still be on the hill.
fieldNote: More warning lets Sara plan a **shift in income** toward holiday lets.
She still expects **lamb prices** and payments to fall, so stays anxious.
Her **community spirit** shows in worry for older neighbours.
She'd adopt AI only after seeing **a neighbour** use it well.

steps.text: Add a second holiday let in the old cart shed by 2030
Use AI booking and form tools once a neighbour proves them
Save monthly toward Hana's vet school fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to prepare properly. I'd say hill farms will be the last place robots work well, because nothing on a hill is flat or simple. I'd be calmer saying it than in the other pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the hills buy us more time than the card says. But the payments are still my worry, because the AI in the government office would arrive in 2036 whatever happens on the hill. By 2039 I'd be 56, and if the payments and lamb prices both fall, it's still a struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep farming as now, flock and cattle the same. I'd keep building up the holiday let slowly, from savings and not loans, since there's no rush. And I'd plan Hana's and Adam's studies so neither of them depends on the hill to make a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious underneath, but steadier. Ten years feels like a season you can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hills buy time. Is that a hope or something you've seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. The lowland farms already have machines that steer themselves, and none of them would last a week on our hill. But I'm not an engineer, so I can't promise it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could ask the government for one thing in this picture, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep paying hill farms for looking after the land, and have a person check our claims, not a machine. That's all. We don't want handouts on the hill farms, we want to be paid fairly for real work.

say: Ten years is enough for **families to prepare** properly.
**Hill farms** will be the last place robots work well.
think: The hills buy **more time** than the card says.
**Payments** remain my worry, since AI in government arrives in 2036 anyway.
do: Keep the **flock and cattle** the same in the first year.
Build up the **holiday let** slowly from savings, not loans.
Plan the children's studies so **neither depends** on the hill.
feel: **Anxious underneath** but steadier, like a season to plan for.
S4.quote: We don't want handouts on the hill farms, we want to be paid fairly for real work.
fieldNote: Sara believes **steep hill land** delays robots, but admits she can't be sure.
The **payment office** remains her steady fear in every picture.
She rejects **handouts** but wants fair pay for land stewardship.
She'd prepare her children for **work beyond the farm**.

steps.text: Keep 650 ewes and 40 suckler cows as now
Expand the holiday let slowly from savings, not loans
Plan Hana's and Adam's studies for careers beyond the hill

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the payment office and the robots would hit us within a few years of each other, with the children still at school. What would help is a promise that hill payments carry on for a fixed number of years, with a real person checking claims, so families like ours can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Our community at the mosque would carry us through hard times, the way the church carries other families. People who have that will cope better than people who are on their own.

headlineQuote: Our community at the mosque would carry us through hard times, the way the church carries other families.
portrait: Sara Ibrahim is a 43-year-old **hill sheep farmer** with 650 ewes, 40 cows and two children.
Her worry in every picture is the **hill payments**, which have been cut twice already.
She fears **AI** in the **payment office** more than AI on her own farm.
Her answer is a **holiday let** and family working together, not government help.
She uses AI **now and then**, after seeing it proven by others.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with payments and robots hitting within a few years of each other.
whatWouldHelp: A **fixed-term promise** on hill payments, with a person checking claims.
